verbatim: The ﬁeld studies were conducted over a two–year period from (2012–2014). The ﬁrst cropping cycle was from July to November 2012, the second cropping cycle span from December 2012 to March/April 2013, the third cropping cycle from July to November 2013, and the fourth cropping cycle was from December 2013-March/April 2014. Thus, there were 4 cropping cycles in all.

claim: The Kpong trial ran four cropping cycles: July-November 2012, December 2012-March/April 2013, July-November 2013 and December 2013-March/April 2014.

verbatim: Figure 1. Dynamics of minimum and maximum temperatures over the cropping period (2012–2014) at Kpong, Ghana. The 1st and 3rd cropping cycles were from July to November while the 2nd and 4th cropping cycles spanned the period December to April.

claim: At Kpong, the 2nd and 4th cropping cycles spanned December to April (so cycle 2 ended April 2013 and cycle 4 April 2014), while cycles 1 and 3 ran July to November.

verbatim: For the current study, we used rice husk as a feedstock to produce biochar with a Japanese retort kiln [33] at a pyrolysis temperature range of between 336 and 394 ◦C (average 360 ◦C).
locator: p. 3, Section 2.2 Biochar Production and Characterization, para 1
claim: The biochar applied at Kpong was rice husk biochar made in a Japanese retort kiln at 336-394 degC (average 360 degC).

verbatim: The charring resulted in 61% weight loss (biochar yield of 39%). The charred husk (biochar) was spread out and water sprayed and allowed to be sun dried. Further details on the kiln can be found in [14]. The biochar was ground and sieved with a 0.5 mm size sieve
locator: p. 3, Section 2.2, para 1
claim: Charring rice husk in the retort kiln gave a biochar yield of 39% (61% weight loss) and the biochar was sieved to 0.5 mm.

verbatim: At the end of each cropping cycle, about 40 tons of rice husk is disposed of by burning at SIREC.
locator: p. 3, Section 2.2, para 1
claim: At SIREC about 40 tons of rice husk is disposed of by burning at the end of each cropping cycle, the feedstock source for the biochar.

verbatim: The biochar was spread and incorporated into a depth of 10 cm of the topsoil. The subplots were replicated three times and completely randomized in each main plot. Each subplot measured 3.5 m × 4.5 m (15.75 m2) with 1 m border space between plots.
locator: p. 4, Section 2.3, para 2
claim: At Kpong the biochar was incorporated to 10 cm, each N subplot (3.5 m x 4.5 m, 15.75 m2) was replicated three times and completely randomized within each main plot.

verbatim: After the biochar application, the plots were allowed to stabilize for a week after which they were ﬂooded a day prior to rice transplanting. Rice (cv KRC Baika) was transplanted at a spacing of 20 cm × 20 cm with four seedlings and later thinned to two per stand at 10 days after transplanting. Two weeks after transplanting, half of the N rate were applied as N P K with P and K being their oxide forms (P2O5 and K2O, respectively) to each of the N treatments. The remaining of the aforementioned N rates were applied as urea top up at 5 weeks after transplanting on the respective plots.
locator: p. 4, Section 2.3, para 2
claim: Both biochar and no-biochar plots were flooded, transplanted with rice cv KRC Baika at 20 x 20 cm, and given the same N rate split as NPK at 2 weeks and urea at 5 weeks after transplanting.

verbatim: At maturity, an area of 1.6 m × 1.6 m in the middle of each plot was harvested and the above ground biomass was separated into the grains and straw.
locator: p. 4, Section 2.4 Plant and Soil Sampling and Analysis, para 1
claim: Grain and straw yield at Kpong were measured by harvesting 1.6 m x 1.6 m in the middle of each plot at maturity.

verbatim: The weather patterns varied with sowing time. In particular, the temperatures were lower during the 1st and 3rd cropping cycles than the 2nd and 4th cropping cycles (Figure 1).
locator: p. 6, Section 3.1 Temperatures during Cropping Cycles
claim: At Kpong, temperatures were lower in the 1st and 3rd cropping cycles (July-November 2012 and 2013) than in the 2nd and 4th (December-April 2013 and 2014).

verbatim: During the 2nd cropping cycle, the minimum temperature was between 24 ◦C in January and 25 ◦C in March whereas maximum temperatures ranged from 33.3 ◦C in December to 35.9 ◦C in March. The trend of minimum and maximum temperatures in the 2nd and 4th cropping cycles were similar to those of the 1st and 3rd cropping cycles respectively. Thus, temperatures were generally higher in the 2nd and 4th cropping cycles than those in the 1st and 3rd cropping cycles.
locator: p. 6, Section 3.1
claim: In cycle 2 at Kpong maximum temperatures ranged from 33.3 degC (December) to 35.9 degC (March), and cycles 2 and 4 were generally hotter than cycles 1 and 3.

verbatim: Both straw and grain yields were lower for the second and fourth cropping cycle experiments due to higher temperatures (particularly during the reproductive stage). The high temperature (above 34 ◦C) during the ﬂowering stage could have increased spikelet sterility with a consequential decrease in yield [51].
locator: p. 17, Section 4.3 Straw and Grain Yield, para 3
claim: The authors attribute lower grain and straw yields in cropping cycles 2 and 4 at Kpong to higher temperatures (above 34 degC at flowering) during the reproductive stage.

verbatim: Applying biochar resulted in yield increases of between 16 and 29% (average 20%) across the various N rates. Similar trends in yield increases in biochar treated plots were observed in the other 3 cropping cycles with average yield increases (across N rates) ranging between 14 and 17%.
locator: p. 11, Section 3.4 Straw and Grain Yield, para 1
claim: At Kpong, adding 10 t/ha biochar raised rice grain yield by 16-29% (average 20%) across N rates in cycle 1 and by an average 14-17% across N rates in cycles 2-4, relative to the same N rate without biochar.

locator: p. 2, Section 2.5 Biochar Preparation and Application
claim: The biochar in the Guto Gida trial was made from maize cob in a pit and sieved to 2 mm particle size.

locator: p. 3, Section 2.5
claim: Biochar was applied to the topsoil in charged (water-soaked) form in the Guto Gida trial.

verbatim: Urea (CO(NH2)2) was applied at 200 kg·ha−1 in split form; that is, half of the recommended dose (100 kg·ha−1) was applied during planting, whereas the remaining half (100 kg·ha−1) was applied 40 days after planting. Biochar was applied one week prior to planting as per the treatment levels, charged, and mixed with the soil to reduce from wind uptake. Inorganic NPS fertilizer was applied at the rate (0, 60, and 120 g plot−1) depending on the treatment at the time of planting, and the remaining cultural and agronomic practices were applied uniformly for all treatments according to their recommendations.
locator: p. 2, Section 2.4 Experimental Procedure
claim: In the 2020 Guto Gida trial all plots received 200 kg/ha urea split at planting and 40 DAP, biochar was applied one week before planting, NPS at planting, and all other practices uniformly across treatments.

verbatim: The legume fallow experiment/technology involved planting maize in the major season in between March and April and relaying a legume in the maize as a cover crop. The legume is relayed between June and July, usually 5–8 weeks after planting maize depending on the time of planting and legume species, earlier for non-creeping and later for creeping legumes to avoid strangling of the maize crop. The maize is harvested about 12–16 weeks after planting, and both ﬁelds with and without legumes are left under fallow for about eight months to go through the dry season. In the second season the legume/cover crop and natural fallow (on the control plot) were cleared between February and March and planted to maize, which was harvested between August and September (see Figure 1: diagonal lines show the range of planting and harvesting dates).
locator: p. 7 [printed p. 275], Description of legume fallow experiments, para 1
claim: Season-1 maize was planted March-April with the legume relayed June-July (5-8 weeks after maize planting), both legume and control fields were left fallow about eight months through the dry season, and in season 2 the fallows were cleared February-March and planted to maize harvested August-September.

verbatim: Five herbaceous legume fallow treatments with Mucuna pruriens, Lablab purpureus, Stylosanthes spp., Pueraria phaseoloides and Canavalia spp. and a control were compared. The control treatment is the traditional/farmer’s practice with no legume. No inorganic fertilizer was applied as farmers do not normally use this in maize cultivation in the study areas.
locator: p. 7 [printed p. 275], Description of legume fallow experiments, para 1
claim: Five herbaceous legume fallow treatments (Mucuna pruriens, Lablab purpureus, Stylosanthes spp., Pueraria phaseoloides, Canavalia spp.) were compared with a no-legume farmer-practice control, with no inorganic fertiliser applied to any arm.

verbatim: Farmers sowed 2 kg of maize on variable plot sizes in lines between March and April at a spacing of 80 × 50 cm with 2–3 seeds per hole in lines. The mean farmer maize plot size was 0.3 (0.1–0.6) ha. The intervention plot measuring 40 × 30 m2 (0.12 ha) was marked by researchers and laid within the farmer’s maize ﬁeld. It was demarcated into three treatment plots for legume species 1 and 2 and a control. Each farmer planted two legume species to compare with the control and was supplied with 2 kg of any of the large-seeded legume covers, Mucuna, Canavalia or Lablab, and 60 g of small-seeded species such as Stylosanthes and Pueraria. Creeping legumes (Mucuna spp., Lablab purpureus, Pueraria spp.) were sown on sole maize farms 7–8 weeks after sowing maize to avoid strangling of the maize crop while non-creeping ones (Canavalia ensiformis, Stylosanthes hamata, S. guianensis) were sown on both sole maize and mixed plots (maize-plantain-cassava-cocoyam mix) at 5–6 weeks after sowing maize.
locator: p. 7 [printed p. 275], Description of legume fallow experiments, para 2
claim: Each farmer's 40 x 30 m (0.12 ha) intervention plot inside the maize field was split into two legume plots and a control; farmers received 2 kg of large-seeded or 60 g of small-seeded legume seed; creeping legumes were sown 7-8 weeks and non-creeping legumes 5-6 weeks after maize sowing.
